questions.question: What is vertical scaling?
options: Adding more machines to a cluster
Upgrading a single machine with more CPU, RAM, or storage
Distributing data across multiple data centers
Adding more network bandwidth between servers
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling (scaling up) means making a single machine more powerful by adding CPU cores, RAM, faster disks, etc. It's simple but has hard limits — the biggest machine money can buy still has a ceiling, and costs increase exponentially near that ceiling.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling?
options: Making a single server taller by stacking more hardware
Adding more machines to a system so work is spread across them
Increasing the clock speed of existing processors
Doubling the RAM in every server
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scaling out) means adding more machines to handle increased load. Instead of one powerful server, you use many commodity servers working together. This is how companies like Google and Netflix handle billions of requests.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the 8 Fallacies of Distributed Computing?
options: The CPU is always the bottleneck
The network is reliable
All servers run the same operating system
Databases never lose data
questions.explanation: 'The network is reliable' is the first and most impactful fallacy. In reality, networks drop packets, experience variable latency, and suffer outages. Designing a distributed system without accounting for network unreliability leads to subtle, hard-to-debug production failures.

questions.question: What is a network partition in distributed systems?
options: Dividing a network into VLANs for security
A failure where some nodes can communicate with each other but not with certain other nodes
Splitting a database table into multiple partitions
Physically cutting network cables during maintenance
questions.explanation: A network partition occurs when the network splits into disconnected groups — nodes within each group can communicate, but nodes across groups cannot. During a partition, the system must decide whether to remain available (serve potentially stale data) or consistent (refuse requests).

questions.question: Why does the cost of vertical scaling increase exponentially as you approach hardware limits?
options: Software license fees increase with server size
High-end components use cutting-edge technology with low yields and limited supply, driving prices up disproportionately
Electricity costs double with each CPU core added
Operating systems charge more for servers with more RAM
questions.explanation: Near the top of the hardware capability curve, components use the latest fabrication processes with lower manufacturing yields. A server with 2x the cores and RAM of a commodity machine often costs 5-10x more due to specialized components, limited competition, and engineering complexity.

questions.question: The fallacy 'latency is zero' leads to which common architectural mistake?
options: Using too many CPU cores
Making many fine-grained remote calls between services, not accounting for network round-trip time
Using SSDs instead of HDDs
Writing logs to disk instead of keeping them in memory
questions.explanation: When developers assume latency is zero, they design chatty interfaces with many small remote calls — the same way they'd call local functions. Each call adds network round-trip time (often 0.5-100+ ms), and hundreds of small calls can make a single operation take seconds. Batching and coarse-grained APIs mitigate this.

questions.question: What makes partial failure unique to distributed systems compared to single-machine systems?
options: Single machines never fail
In distributed systems, some components can fail while others continue working, creating ambiguous states where you may not know if a remote operation succeeded
Partial failure only affects the network, never the application
Partial failure means the system runs at half speed
questions.explanation: On a single machine, failures are typically total — the process crashes and you know it. In distributed systems, a remote call might timeout: did the server crash, is the network slow, or did the operation succeed but the response got lost? This ambiguity makes error handling fundamentally more complex.

questions.question: A single-server database handles 10,000 queries per second. Traffic grows to 50,000 QPS. You could buy a server 5x more powerful for $50,000/month, or add 5 commodity servers at $3,000/month each. What is the monthly cost difference, and what trade-off do you accept with horizontal scaling?
options: $35,000/month saved with horizontal scaling, but you accept the complexity of distributing queries and handling partial failures across 5 nodes
$5,000/month saved with vertical scaling, with no additional complexity
No cost difference; both approaches cost the same
$15,000/month saved with horizontal scaling, with no trade-offs
questions.explanation: Horizontal: 5 x $3,000 = $15,000/month. Vertical: $50,000/month. Savings: $35,000/month. But horizontal scaling requires load balancing, data partitioning, handling partial failures, and distributed coordination — significantly more engineering complexity. The cost savings are real, but so is the operational burden.

questions.question: During a network partition, a distributed database with 5 nodes splits into a group of 3 and a group of 2. If the system prioritizes consistency, what happens to the group of 2?
options: It continues serving reads and writes normally
It stops accepting writes (and possibly reads) because it cannot form a majority quorum
It automatically promotes itself to the primary cluster
It deletes all its data to prevent inconsistency
questions.explanation: In a consistency-first system using majority quorum (3 out of 5), the partition with only 2 nodes cannot reach quorum. It must stop accepting writes to prevent divergent state. The partition with 3 nodes can form a majority and continues operating. This is the consistency vs. availability trade-off during partitions.

questions.question: Which of the 8 fallacies of distributed computing is MOST often violated when a team migrates from a monolith to microservices for the first time?
options: The network is secure
Latency is zero — teams treat remote service calls like local function calls, not accounting for network overhead
There is one administrator
The network is homogeneous
questions.explanation: Teams new to microservices often decompose a monolith into many small services connected by synchronous HTTP calls. What was a nanosecond in-process function call becomes a millisecond network round trip. A single user request might trigger dozens of inter-service calls, each adding latency, timeout risk, and failure modes.
